questions.q: What two adjustments does this lesson recommend when presenting SR-5 in an actual onsite loop, versus the Lesson 15 classroom-style presentation?
options: Remove all risk and limitations content, and never allow questions
Expect to be interrupted with challenging questions mid-presentation, and have a compressed 3-minute version ready in case you're asked for the short version first
Present only the gross Sharpe and skip the net number entirely
Read the full written report aloud word for word
questions.explain: An onsite loop involves far more interruption than a classroom setting, and interview slots are often shorter, so a compressed 3-minute version (hypothesis, net result, one risk caveat, one limitation) should be ready.

questions.q: What are the five steps of the recommended case-interview framework, in order?
options: Guess an answer, defend it, move on
Clarify the objective, state assumptions explicitly, propose a structure, reason about what could go wrong, conclude with a clear recommendation and caveats
State the recommendation first, then work backward to justify it
Ask the interviewer to answer their own question
questions.explain: The five-step framework moves from clarifying the actual objective through stated assumptions, a proposed structure, risk reasoning, and a concrete final recommendation.

questions.q: If a colleague shows you a strategy backtest with a Sharpe of 3.0, what is the recommended first reaction, and why?
options: Immediate excitement and congratulations, since a high Sharpe is always good news

Scrutiny before celebration — ask whether it's gross or net, check for look-ahead bias, survivorship bias, and overfitting, since SR-5's own gross Sharpe of 0.76 is a more typical number for this kind of strategy
Assume the number must be a typo and ignore it
Accept it at face value as long as the colleague seems confident
questions.explain: An unusually high Sharpe like 3.0 should trigger scrutiny for common failure modes (look-ahead bias, survivorship bias, overfitting, unmodeled costs) before any excitement, especially against SR-5's own believable gross Sharpe of 0.76.

questions.q: How should a take-home assignment be approached, according to this lesson?
options: Oversell the result to make the write-up more impressive
Treat it like the Lesson 13 performance report: state hypothesis and method clearly, show gross and net results where relevant, include an honest limitations section, and submit on time
Skip the write-up entirely and submit only code
Submit late if needed to make the result look more polished
questions.explain: A take-home is graded on both the result and the write-up — an honest, on-time submission with a limitations section reads far better than a late submission that oversells a shaky result.

questions.q: What is 'look-ahead bias' in the context of a quant case interview?
options: A bias toward choosing strategies with longer backtest periods
Using information in a backtest that would not actually have been available at the time a decision was made
A preference for forward-looking rather than historical data
The tendency of interviewers to look ahead at a candidate's resume before meeting them
questions.explain: Look-ahead bias means a backtest used information not actually available at that point in time — one of the standard culprits to check when a backtest result looks suspiciously strong.
